"Fain" means willing — but it's a specific, layered kind of willingness. It sits somewhere between eager and content to accept. There are two closely related shades of meaning, and understanding both is the key to truly knowing this word.

Here, "fain" describes someone who actually wants to do something — they're glad and ready. Think of it as a literary, old-fashioned way of saying "happy to," "glad to," or "eager to."

"She was fain to share her news with the world."
→ She was genuinely eager and happy to share it.

"The young knight was fain to prove his worth."
→ He was willing — even enthusiastic — to prove himself.
Sense 2: Willing Because There's No Better Option

This is the more nuanced sense, and it's where "fain" earns its real depth. Here, the person isn't enthusiastically eager — they're willing to settle for something because circumstances leave them little choice. They accept it, they're at peace with it, but there's a quiet undertone of "this isn't ideal, but I'll take it."

"With no shelter in sight, the traveler was fain to sleep under the open sky."
→ He had no better option, so he was willing — even content — to make do.

"She was fain to accept whatever work came her way."
→ She had little choice, so she accepted whatever was available.

The key distinction between the two senses:
In Sense 1, the person wants to do the thing.
In Sense 2, they have to do the thing, and they've made their peace with it.
Both involve willingness — just different origins of that willingness.

As an adjective, "fain" almost always follows a single, specific pattern:

[Subject] + [was/is/were] + fain + to + [verb]

  • "He was fain to agree."
  • "They were fain to leave."
  • "She was fain to obey."

You won't see someone called "a fain person" the way you'd say "a happy person." It doesn't sit before a noun. It always attaches to an action, via "to."

"Fain" is notably quiet and calm. It doesn't carry the intensity of words like desperate or determined. It belongs to someone who has settled into their situation and is genuinely at peace with what they must do — whether driven by desire or by necessity.

Picture someone who has been walking all day and finally finds a modest inn. They weren't hoping for luxury, but they are fain to stop there. Not overjoyed — just willing, calm, and ready to accept it.

"Fain" is archaic — it belongs to older English and is almost entirely absent from modern everyday speech. You'll encounter it in:

  • Classic literature — Shakespeare, Milton, Keats, Spenser
  • Historical fiction deliberately written in an old-fashioned voice
  • Poetry, especially from the Renaissance or Romantic periods
  • Formal or highly elevated writing

If you come across it outside these contexts, it would be an intentional stylistic choice to evoke an old-world or literary tone.
Everything in One Place: A Final Summary

Fain (adjective) = willing, eager, or content to do something — either because you genuinely want to (Sense 1), or because circumstances have left you no better option and you've accepted that (Sense 2). It always points toward an action using the pattern "was fain to [do something]" and carries a tone of quiet, composed willingness rather than loud enthusiasm. It is an archaic word, found almost exclusively in older or literary English.
